title: "GRC Frameworks & Risk Management"
order: 81

## The finish line

By the end of this course you can run a system or process through a full
categorize→select→implement→assess→authorize→monitor cycle, track its open deficiencies the way
a POA&M (plan of action and milestones) does, and say in one sentence why that whole motion is
the same decision Lakeshore already makes every time it releases a validated system or runs a
periodic review. This is the course where "GRC" (Governance, Risk, and Compliance) stops being a
buzzword your CIO uses and becomes a framework you can actually run.

This course borrows its structure from NIST's Risk Management Framework (RMF) — built for U.S.
federal information systems, never a legal requirement for a private blood establishment like
Lakeshore — the same way this curriculum has already borrowed ICH Q9's structure for quality risk
and AABB's accreditation structure for assessment readiness. The point isn't that Lakeshore is
suddenly a federal agency. It's that RMF names, with unusual precision, a motion you already run
informally: decide how much a system matters, pick safeguards sized to that, build them, check
they actually work, decide the residual risk is acceptable, and keep checking. One vocabulary,
spoken fluently, instead of three different ones for quality, security, and validation.

## Before you start

This course assumes the foundations and two earlier Track 2/3 courses:

- [Reading a CFR citation](../../foundations/reading-a-cfr-citation/index.qmd),
  [Regulatory landscape orientation](../../foundations/regulatory-landscape-orientation/index.qmd),
  and [Risk and controls vocabulary](../../foundations/risk-and-controls-vocabulary/index.qmd) —
  likelihood/severity/detectability and inherent-versus-residual risk are assumed fluent, not
  re-taught.
- [Quality System Essentials](../quality-system-essentials/index.qmd), especially
  [Quality risk management](../quality-system-essentials/quality-risk-management/index.qmd)
  (ICH Q9(R1)'s own four-stage process and its FMEA/Risk-Ranking-and-Filtering toolkit — already
  built in depth; this course names it again only to compare it, never to re-teach it) and
  [CAPA](../quality-system-essentials/index.qmd) (root cause through effectiveness check — the
  direct parallel this course's final module draws against a POA&M).
- [CSV & BECS](../csv-and-becs/index.qmd), for the validation lifecycle (IQ/OQ/PQ, periodic
  review) this course's own closing module says is "the same motion" as an authorization
  decision.

## The five modules

Each module is one sitting, and each has its own finish line.

1. **Risk management frameworks side by side.** Put NIST's Risk Management Framework, ISO 31000,
   and ICH Q9 next to each other, and show they're the same underlying motion — identify risk,
   decide on a response, implement it, verify it, accept the residual risk, keep watching — in
   three different vocabularies, issued by three very different kinds of body.
2. **Categorize and select controls.** Apply RMF's own first two steps to a real Lakeshore
   system: decide how much a system actually matters (its impact if confidentiality, integrity,
   or availability failed), then select and tailor a set of controls sized to that, not a
   one-size-fits-all checklist.
3. **Implement and assess controls.** Build the controls the previous module selected, then run
   an independent assessment of whether they actually work — the security-risk equivalent of a
   validation study, run by someone who didn't build the thing they're checking.
4. **Authorize and monitor.** Make and document the authorization decision itself — accepting a
   named residual risk, on the record, the way an Authorizing Official does — and build the
   ongoing monitoring plan that keeps that decision honest after go-live. Say, in one sentence,
   why this is the same decision as a validation release followed by periodic review.
5. **Tracking remediation: POA&Ms next to CAPAs.** Take every control gap the assessment
   surfaced and track it to closure on a POA&M, then place that instrument next to a CAPA and
   show they're doing the identical job — prioritized, dated remediation with real
   accountability — in two different vocabularies.

## A note on sources

- **NIST SP 800-37 Rev 2** (public, U.S. government work, free to quote verbatim) supplies RMF's
  seven steps (Prepare, Categorize, Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize, Monitor — Prepare is
  named honestly as Rev 2's own addition, not folded silently into the curriculum's own six-step
  framing), the authorization-to-operate concept, and the POA&M discussion. Quoted from a saved,
  scoped excerpt — never the full 183-page document from memory.
- **ISO 31000** (a paid international standard) is named and its themes described in this
  course's own words — never quoted, the same handling this curriculum already gives AABB
  Standards, GAMP 5, and ISO 19011.
- **ICH Q9(R1)** is never re-taught here — only named as the third point of comparison, pointing
  back to `quality-risk-management` for the actual content.
- No new CFR, FDA guidance, or AABB material is introduced in this course; it sits one level up,
  in the risk-framework vocabulary that sits over all of them.

Modules appear in the sidebar as they're built.
